title: THE MARRIAGE BED IS NOT DIRTY: What Hebrews Actually Says About Sex and Honor
paragraphs:
THE MARRIAGE BED IS NOT DIRTY: What Hebrews Actually Says About Sex and Honor
Some Christians learned to feel ashamed of something God Himself called honorable—and Hebrews 13:4 may not be saying what shame taught you to hear.
There are married Christians who love Jesus deeply…
who genuinely want to honor God…
and yet when the bedroom door closes, something strange happens inside them.
A feeling they cannot quite explain.
They know they are married. They know they love each other. They know they have made covenant promises before God.
But somewhere along the way, they absorbed an idea that Scripture itself never taught:
That holiness means becoming almost embarrassed by physical desire.
That truly spiritual Christians should tolerate marital intimacy rather than delight in it.
And sometimes nobody ever explicitly told them this.
Through sermons that spoke extensively about sexual sin but almost never explained God's beautiful purpose for sexual intimacy.
So some believers learned what Christianity says “no” to without ever understanding the holy “yes” that makes the “no” meaningful.
And then Hebrews says something astonishing.
Not as though God is embarrassed by what happens between a husband and wife.
The Greek text of Hebrews 13:4 reads:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
Marriage is to be honored, and the marriage bed is undefiled.
The same basic Greek word family can describe something regarded as precious or of great value.
And then Scripture uses a surprisingly physical word:
The word can refer literally to a bed and, depending on context, carries the unmistakable association of sexual relations.
Then comes the word that generations of shame desperately need to hear:
Hebrews does not say the marriage bed is a necessary contamination that God reluctantly permits.
Because Christianity's sexual ethic was never supposed to teach us that sex itself is filthy.
Scripture teaches something much more beautiful—and much more demanding.
Sexual intimacy has a God-given place.
And because that place is precious, violating it matters.
The verse does not end with the marriage bed.
It continues by warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
The biblical logic is much closer to:
Marriage is honorable. The marriage bed is undefiled. Therefore do not desecrate God's gift through sexual immorality and adultery.
The boundary exists because what is inside the boundary matters.
And this reaches much further back than Hebrews.
Before human civilization had developed elaborate sexual customs…
Then Scripture says something our shame-filled generation sometimes races past:
“The man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
Sexual embodiment was not invented by Satan.
The human body was God's idea.
Male and female were God's idea.
The possibility of husband and wife becoming “one flesh” existed within God's good creation.
Because Satan's strategy has never required him to invent everything from nothing.
He often corrupts something God created good.
And sexual desire can become lust, exploitation, adultery, pornography, fornication, selfishness, manipulation, and idolatry.
But abuse of a gift does not prove the gift was evil.
It proves the human heart desperately needs redemption.
This is where some people reading this may suddenly become uncomfortable.
Because perhaps your struggle is not theological.
Maybe sex feels dirty because somebody made it dirty for you.
Maybe your first exposure to sexuality was pornography rather than covenant.
Maybe someone touched what they had no right to touch.
Maybe someone used Scripture to control you.
Maybe you carried secret pornography into marriage and discovered that marriage does not magically erase lust.
Maybe you crossed boundaries years ago and still cannot forgive yourself.
Maybe you have confessed the sin to God a hundred times, yet every time you think about your past, another voice begins whispering:
“God tolerates you now, but you will never really be clean.”
That voice is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not pretend sin is harmless.
Jesus never needed to minimize sin in order to maximize grace.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that Christ died.
Grace is so astonishing that Christ died for sinners.
There is an enormous difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction brings darkness into the light so that Christ can heal, forgive, cleanse, and transform.
Condemnation keeps pointing backward as though the blood of Jesus accomplished nothing.
The Gospel says something far more powerful than “your choices don't matter.”
The Gospel says your sin mattered so much that the Son of God carried judgment—and His grace is so powerful that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is why the theme of Scripture is never merely behavior modification.
But grace never means calling darkness light.
The very verse that calls the marriage bed undefiled also says God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
We cannot keep half of Hebrews 13:4 and erase the other half.
God also takes covenant betrayal seriously.
Both truths come from the same holy God.
That means “the marriage bed is undefiled” is not a blank check for selfishness.
Marriage does not transform every desire into righteousness simply because two people possess a marriage certificate.
Biblical intimacy still belongs beneath the lordship of Jesus.
The dignity of your spouse matters.
It is not an entitlement to be seized.
It is not an object through which another person reenacts pornography.
Christian marriage is not permission to become selfish behind a locked bedroom door.
Perhaps nowhere is this clearer than in 1 Corinthians 7, where Paul speaks with striking mutuality.
The husband has responsibilities toward his wife.
The wife has responsibilities toward her husband.
Paul's language repeatedly moves in both directions.
In a world where women could easily be treated as possessions, that mutuality is significant.
Biblical marital intimacy is not supposed to communicate:
“I have given myself to you in covenant love.”
And that is why pornography is such a devastating counterfeit.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume bodies without covenant.
It offers pleasure detached from responsibility.
“What can this body do for me?”
“How can I love this person faithfully?”
And suddenly the bedroom becomes far more theological than many Christians realized.
Because Christian marriage points beyond itself.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 about husband and wife, then suddenly declares:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Not because every marriage perfectly represents Jesus.
But covenant faithfulness whispers something about the Bridegroom who refuses to abandon His bride.
Jesus does not consume His bride.
He does not exploit her weakness.
So when a husband chooses tenderness instead of selfishness…
when a wife chooses faithfulness instead of fantasy…
when two wounded people learn patience with one another…
when pornography is confessed and abandoned…
when betrayal is confronted rather than hidden…
when forgiveness is sought rather than presumed upon…
when years of shame slowly surrender to biblical truth…
something larger than sex is happening.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear.
Not permission to justify whatever desire happens to exist inside you.
But permission to stop calling dirty what God created for covenant.
Culture says sex can become ultimate.
Shame says sex is inherently filthy.
Scripture places sexuality underneath something infinitely greater:
Your sexual history is not your savior.
Your ability to maintain a spotless reputation is not your savior.
And this matters enormously for the person whose story is already broken.
Maybe you lived with someone outside marriage.
Maybe you gave away pieces of yourself because you desperately wanted to feel loved.
Maybe you knowingly rebelled against God.
Repentance is not God standing at the door waiting to humiliate you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who already knows the entire story.
You will never shock Jesus with the chapter you are afraid to tell Him.
At the cross, Christ did not die for the edited version of you.
First Corinthians 6 contains one of the New Testament's strongest warnings concerning sexual sin, but then Paul speaks words that should stop every ashamed sinner in their tracks.
After naming serious sins, he tells believers:
“You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Your past can describe where grace found you without defining where grace is taking you.
Your past can describe where grace found you without defining where grace is taking you.
It does not automatically repair a shattered marriage.
It does not make trauma disappear overnight.
It does not mean trust must instantly return after betrayal.
It does not remove the need for confession, accountability, wise pastoral care, counseling where appropriate, boundaries, restitution, or long seasons of rebuilding.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace is discovering that what happened does not have greater authority than Jesus.
This is why Christians desperately need a theology of sexuality that contains both holiness and healing.
Truth without grace can crush wounded people.
Grace without truth can leave enslaved people comfortably chained.
The Savior who told sinners to leave sin is the Savior who welcomed sinners nobody else wanted near the table.
The Savior who exposed darkness is the Savior who carried sinners' shame to Calvary.
He does not merely tell the adulterer, the sexually broken, the porn-addicted, or the ashamed person:
And perhaps this article has exposed another problem.
Some married Christians have been so frightened of sexual sin that they have unintentionally become frightened of marital intimacy itself.
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος… καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος.
God is not embarrassed by a faithful husband loving his wife.
God is not embarrassed by a faithful wife desiring her husband.
The Song of Songs should have settled that embarrassment long ago.
Scripture can speak poetically, joyfully, and tenderly about marital desire without turning sexuality into an idol.

There can even be healing here when husband and wife learn to see each other not through the distorted lens of pornography, comparison, past partners, unrealistic expectations, or shame—but as people made in God's image and entrusted to one another in covenant.
One spouse may desire intimacy more frequently than the other.
And suddenly marriage requires something pornography never teaches:
Love remembers a soul lives inside it.
That is why Christian sexual ethics cannot be reduced to a list of prohibited acts.
Does the way I love reflect the character and lordship of Christ?
For the unmarried Christian, Hebrews 13:4 matters just as deeply.
Honoring marriage means refusing to take covenant privileges while rejecting covenant responsibility.
Biblical boundaries are not God trying to keep pleasure away from you.
They reveal that sexuality is powerful enough to deserve covenant.
And Christians should stop pretending otherwise.
But chastity is not hatred of sexuality.
Biblical chastity recognizes sexuality as significant enough not to trivialize.
And for the married Christian, purity does not suddenly become irrelevant at the wedding.
With what you watch when nobody else is awake.
A ring cannot make an unguarded heart faithful.
Only surrender to Christ can keep transforming the heart.
So perhaps Hebrews 13:4 needs to become more than a verse quoted at people.
Maybe it needs to become a mirror.
What have you been calling dirty that God calls honorable?
And what have you been calling harmless that God calls sin?
Those are two very different questions.
Maybe some people need freedom from shame tonight.
“Stop bringing what is unholy into it.”
Some need to forgive themselves after Christ has forgiven them.
Others need to stop using “grace” as camouflage for secret rebellion.
Most of us probably need some measure of both.
But every road back leads to the same Person.
Not pretending your past never happened.
The crucified Christ who knows exactly what happened.
The risen Christ who refuses to leave repentant sinners inside the graveyard of their former lives.
Seek help where help is needed.
And if shame has convinced you that God could never make anything beautiful from your story, look at the cross.
Christianity itself is the announcement that God can take the scene that appears to be the ultimate catastrophe and make it the doorway through which redemption comes.
If this article uncovered something you have never been able to say aloud, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Someone reading the same comments may discover they are not the only believer still fighting for healing, purity, restoration, and a marriage centered on Christ.
Not because every sentence will be needed today.
Because there may come a night when shame returns, temptation whispers, your marriage feels exhausted, or someone you love finally admits what they have been hiding.
You may need these Scriptures again.

Grace cannot be bought. But supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work can be one practical way to help biblical teaching reach another wounded marriage, another struggling believer, another person secretly wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
Invite your spouse. Invite your family. Even send this to the skeptic who thinks Christianity only knows how to speak about sex through shame.
And if you want to go deeper and support the mission:
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the distinction Hebrews refuses to let us forget.
God does not call sexual sin holy.
But neither does He call the marriage bed dirty.
He calls the marriage bed undefiled.
He calls sexual immorality to judgment.
And He calls sinners to repentance, cleansing, forgiveness, and new life through Jesus Christ.
So stop asking whether your past is ugly enough to defeat grace.
Ask whether the blood of Jesus is powerful enough to cleanse sinners.
Your darkest chapter may explain your scars, but it does not get to write the ending when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
